Film, to a lesser extent your eye, and to an even lesser extent a CCD, are all activated by photons and hold that charge for a nonzero time. We can consider that time to be "forever" for film and "doesn't matter because the brain only counts the first time unless you are seeing LSD tracers" for the eye.

The camera flash could be considered as a shotgun shell full of photons. As far as we can see they all arrive at once. In reality there is a ramp up and ramp down time where some lead, some trail, and the majority fall in the middle. If the shutter is open all of them arriving at that time reach the film, whether it was open for a minute or a millisecond.

Cheap cameras and your eye can be considered to always have the shutter open. The photons charge rods and cones or charge the camera's sensor. This charge hangs out for a while, and I won't pretend I know how long, it's more than 10 seconds for the eye, probably milliseconds for older sensors, probably nanoseconds for newer ones. The brain registers it then filters it out. Cameras use software algorithms which can account for outliers. If one line in the rolling shutter read is too far from the ones surrounding it, the data may be discarded and smoothed.

Film doesn't have that ability so shutter speed matters there, that's why your description didn't work. The read time on the device is faster than the framerate so it's entirely possible to have the flash occur outside the time the sensor is read, or over a small enough area it's discarded as an outlier.

You've seen videos where wheels or helicopter blades appear stationary. This happens with both types of camera, but the difference is this: The film camera recorded all the photons while the shutter was open. Some software analyzed it in bits and pieces very quickly, but didn't necessarily even know about all the photons.
